newsitem.title: USA: TI CFO sees chip market up 10 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: TI CFO sees chip market up 10 pct in 1997.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc expects the global semiconductor market to grow 10 percent in 1997 despite another recent slump in memory chip prices, Chief Financial Officer Bill Aylesworth said.
"We continue to hold to our forecast of about 10 percent growth for the whole industry that we had earlier this year," Aylesworth told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"We recognize there are some possible downsides to that -- the weakeness of the yen is sort of a negative, and to some degree it will depend on memory prices for the rest of the year -- but 10 (percent) is still our best number," he said.
He said prices for DRAM (dynamic random access memory) chips, which collapsed last year and had only slightly recovered, fell again towards the end of the second quarter.

Aylesworth said supply was outpacing demand and that Texas Instruments was, for example, currently getting about $6.50 for a standard 16-megabyte DRAM chip, down from above $9 early in the second quarter.

"The pressures we saw on DRAM prices starting in mid-June have generally continued and that will continue to put pressure on the performance of the DRAM part of our business in the near term," he said.
He said it was not clear when the memory market would balance out.

"A lot of people with crystal balls are trying to figure that out. We don't have any idea really. A lot of people are saying late this year or early next year but we don't have specific prediction on that," he said.

Despite the problems with memory chips, Texas Instruments earlier on Tuesday reported powerful second quarter earnings, fuelled by higher operating margins and strong sales of newer chips like digital signal processors (DSPs).

TI's second quarter net income soared to $249 million, or $1.26 a share, from $76 million, or $0.39 a share, in the same period last year. Profits from continuing operations and excluding special items jumped to $213 million, or $1.07 a share, from $41 million, or $0.21 a share.
Revenues rose seven percent to $2.56 billion.

"The most positive aspect is continued strong growth and increased profitability in DSP solutions. That business is now more than 40 pct of semiconductor revenues and was the primary reason why we had such good a performarnce in the second quarter," Aylesworth said.
He said wireless products and networking were the hottest areas of the market and the DSP segment of TI's business should continue to grow at about 30 percent per year.
